name: MathlibAnnex.WeakDivergenceZero
title: Vanishing weak gradient tested by divergence

content.display_title: Vanishing weak gradient tested by divergence
content.one_sentence_role: Expresses a weak equation through compactly supported continuously differentiable vector fields.
content.natural_language_statement:
Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed vector space equipped with a measurable structure, let $\mu$ be any measure on $E$, let $U\subseteq E$, and let $u:E\to\mathbb R$. For a $C^1$ vector field $W:E\to E$, write $DW(z)$ for its real Fréchet derivative and $\operatorname{div}W(z)=\operatorname{tr}(DW(z))$. The weak equation considered here is
$$\int_U u(z)\operatorname{div}W(z)\,d\mu(z)=0$$
for every $C^1$ vector field $W:E\to E$ supplied with a compact carrier $K\subseteq U$ containing its nonzero set. The integral is with respect to $\mu|_U$.
content.definition_explanation:
Using $\operatorname{div}W=\operatorname{tr}(DW)$, the complete condition is
$$\forall K\subseteq E\ \text{compact},\quad
\forall W\in C^1(E,E),\quad
\{z:W(z)\ne0\}\subseteq K\subseteq U
\ \Longrightarrow\ 
\int_Uu(z)\operatorname{div}W(z)\,d\mu(z)=0.$$
The source packages $K$ and $W$ together as a compact test field. Without integrability hypotheses, the integral has the total Bochner-integral convention; no distribution-theoretic regularity is silently added.
content.assumptions: The predicate itself assumes no openness of $U$, compatibility between the topology and measurable structure, Haar property of $\mu$, or local integrability of $u$. These are separate hypotheses in its analytic uses. The zero-dimensional case is included.
content.conclusion: The result of the definition is a proposition about $u$, $U$, and $\mu$. It asks for the displayed equality for every admissible pair $(K,W)$, rather than for a derivative of $u$. In the later Haar setting, with $U$ open and $u$ locally integrable on $U$, the compact support and continuous bounded divergence make these test integrals ordinary integrable pairings.
content.lean_realization_notes:
A carrier is a chosen compact containing $\{z:W(z)
e0\}$; it need not equal that set or its closure. Since $E$ is Hausdorff, $K$ is closed and also contains $\overline{\{z:W(z)
e0\}}$. If $z
otin K$, the field is zero on the open neighborhood $E\setminus K$, hence $DW(z)=0$ and $\operatorname{div}W(z)=0$. This neighborhood argument, not merely $W(z)=0$ at one point, confines the divergence to $K$.
